bagel.title: bagel: a parallelizable build system
bagel.body:
Bagel is a lightweight, parallelizable build system written in Rust and C++ that:

  • Builds a dependency DAG and schedules commands to run in topological order
  • Allows incremental builds by skipping up-to-date targets with hashing
  • Supports parallel execution of independent build steps
  • Is inspired by Bazel (Google's build system). This is a fun project, and by no means a production-ready system :)

Introduction

With respect to the design of build systems, Bagel narrows down 3 dimensions of optimization:

  1. Minimality - processing each target only once
  2. Parallelism - executing independent build steps in parallel to reduce overall build times
  3. Incrementality - tracking file changes and dependecy relationships to avoid unnecessary rebuilds on unchanged components

Hermeticity is also an important dimension, but we backlog this in favor for key functionality concerning the other three dimensions. Ideally, we would like to have a container image per language toolchain.

A more detailed discussion can be found in docs/design.md.

Examples

The examples directory contains several demo projects that can be built with Bagel. Here is an example workflow to compare the serial and parallel execution of examples/demo:

cd examples/demo
bagel build --json serial.json
bagel build -j --json parallel.json
cat parallel.json

References

A lot of the design decisions made in this project are based on the following work:

  • Build Systems A La Carte
  • Bazel
  • Buck

Design Rationale

Like all systems, we would like a build system to be efficient. Hence, they are designed around the requirement of minimality. A system is minimal when it can recompute the smallest possible set of values to execute a task. Make relies on hashed file modification times (this alas, can be mutated at will) to decide whether it must rebuild a source file, or do nothing, as it has previously built an equivalent binary.

Overall, you can imagine a build system as a tool that updates your codebase, by systematically executing tasks using information from source files and task description(s). With this, we've defined the invariants of what a build system must do. We have yet to cover how it can choose to do so, which lie in two axioms:

  • How does it discover the correct order to build these files? In the former example, it could not have built main.exe without having built common.o, and we cannot rely on the user to provide a correct ordering for a non-trivial chain of dependencies.
  • How does it know when to avoid re-building a clean file? Remember that we would like this for the sake of minimality.

Build System Axioms

These two choices lie primarily in distinct, but interconnected components:

  1. Scheduler: Orders tasks such that dependencies for any given task exist and are up-to-date before it itself is executed.
  2. Rebuilder: Detects whether a file needs to be rebuilt, and rebuilds it if so.

Some other properties that the design of some of these systems opt-in/out of:

  1. Dynamic dependencies: Given a dependency list a: b, c, if b or c changes, a is automatically recomputed. Excel is an example. This often complicates minimality, as the set of dependencies to recompute are no longer statically defined.

  2. Early cutoff: Tasks often have dependent tasks. If a newly-changed task is executed and produces the same output as the previous task, the build system stops here and does not propagate execution to dependent (parent) tasks.

  3. Remote caching: Most famously attributed to Bazel, caching the source and content hashes of a build is helpful for repeated builds across a large number of related clients. For Google, this means much less time for an individual developer to build an average task, because it's likely someone else has compiled it. Bazel similarly holds the history of all executed commands annotated with observed file hashes to bypass the execution of a task by predicting the hash of the result from its dependencies.

Put together, here is a diagram of build system execution that lists these design choices per component.

Here, Bagel is:

  • Applicative, in terms of how tasks declare dependencies

  • Topological, in terms of how work is scheduled

  • Verifying traces: how an “up-to-date” build is defined

    After a successful build, Bagel caches a hash of the target's inputs, command and env. On the next run it recomputes the hash and skips the target if it matches. This differs from Bazel because we do not store build outputs themselves under their hash.

parlox.title: parlox: a parallel lox interpreter
parlox.body:
parlox is a bytecode interpreter based on Bob Nystrom’s clox from Crafting Interpreters, extended with a split C/Rust memory model.

High-level interpreters face a sharp trade-off between maximizing single-threaded allocation throughput and scaling to multiple cores, and CPython is the classic example: reference counting mutates object headers on every creation, assignment, and destruction. Because these mutations are inherently thread-unsafe, CPython relies on the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), which only lets one thread run bytecode at a time. While the GIL ensures the atomicity of individual instructions, it severely bottlenecks multi-core performance.

Free-threaded CPython (3.13+) makes the GIL optional; however, this breaks a bunch of legacy C extensions (ie. numpy) that assume single-threaded memory access. Instead of ref-counting, parlox uses a thread-safe, tracing, generational GC, leaning on the observation that “most objects die young” such that it never has to scan the whole heap on every cycle.

Why not just write the GC natively in C? Generational collectors involve complex state management (tracing, copying, tenuring, write barriers), which is famously difficult to implement in C. Rust isolates all of the memory state management behind its safety guarantees. For example, Send/Sync traits enforce thread safety without a GIL (incidentally, the same trick tools like PyO3 use for CPython extensions).

The bottleneck here is that C execution engines calling into a Rust GC puts the Foreign Function Interface (FFI) boundary on the critical path, which would negate the point of writing the execution loop in C. So the C VM does zero-overhead allocation with a bump allocator (one pointer addition) inside a pre-allocated Nursery, records live references on a shadow stack, and only crosses the FFI boundary once, in bulk, when the Nursery fills up. Rust then traces the roots, promotes survivors into a Tenured heap, and hands C back a fresh Nursery.

I considered other strategies like conservative stack scanning (scanning the stack and conservatively assuming that anything that happens to look like a pointer, points to a valid heap-allocated object); This approach saves a little overhead on PUSH/POP, but leaks memory through false positives.

I enjoyed working on this primarily to explore PL theory and design, for which the book dives deep into. However, the thesis of the project lies moreso in coupling a cross-language memory model that gets Rust’s memory safety and concurrent garbage collection, without paying FFI latency every time C allocates an object. Anecdotally, the FFI overhead should be negligible enough.

The frontend, VM, and bump allocator are done, and C can call into the Rust crate. I'm currently working on the Rust-side collector.

Ditching thread-unsafe ref-counting also allows for native concurrency! One such paradigm I want to implement is Erlang's Actor Model: instead of sharing memory behind a lock, each C VM runs as an independent actor and threads talk through message passing. Naturally, this involves copying messages, which costs CPU and memory proportional to the message size, but I want to explore how this affects performance in highly concurrent workloads, which I will have to do more instrumentation for.
